title: ASAS-3 (2000-2009) and TESS (2018-2026) data of 3,507 southern eclipsing binaries show vanishing eclipses only in HD 93683 and the new case HD 303514, whose eclipses can stop near 2030
abstract: A third star can turn the orbital plane of a close binary, so that its eclipses fade and stop. We compared ASAS-3 V photometry (2000-2009) with TESS QLP full-frame light curves (2018-2026) for detached and semi-detached binaries of the ASAS Catalogue of Variable Stars. 3,507 stars had usable TESS sectors. Fixed rules flagged 33 stars for lost, emerged or absent eclipses. Visual vetting with the ASAS-3 light curves and all TESS sectors rejected 31: 17 have no coherent ASAS-3 eclipse at the catalogue period, 5 have multi-day eclipses that the detrending removed, and 9 are other variables or have coverage, period, background or counterpart problems. Two systems have eclipses that faded away: the known HD 93683 (positive control) and HD 303514 (TIC 459876082, A4, V = 10.8, P = 19.8972 d), which has no published report of variable eclipses. HD 303514 eclipses were 15-19 percent deep in ASAS-3 in 2002-2005; in TESS the primary fell from 3.07 percent (2019) to 0.74 percent (2026) and the eclipses became narrower. A difference image puts the eclipse on HD 303514. A twin-star model with a linear drift of the impact parameter fits all 15 depths (chi2 = 21 for 12 degrees of freedom), predicts the narrowing with no width parameter (chi2 = 16 against 153 for constant width), and a fit to TESS alone predicts the six ASAS-3 depths (chi2 = 7.2). The widths give (R1+R2)/a = 0.106 and an inclination drift of about 0.10 deg/yr; if the drift stays linear the eclipses stop near 2030 (68 percent range 2029.4-2030.5 over the tested dilutions). Gaia DR3 RUWE = 5.9 agrees with an unseen companion; a rough estimate gives an outer period of a few years. For 302 random ASAS-confirmed binaries the TESS/ASAS depth ratio has median 1.00 (16-84 percent: 0.82-1.23). Both fading systems have P > 17 d: 0 of about 2,580 effective binaries with P <= 10 d lost eclipses (95 percent limit 1.2e-3 in about 20 yr), against 2 of about 110 with P > 10 d. Limits: up to 5 QLP sectors per star, simple detrending, a catalogue amplitude as the old depth, a simple twin model with approximate dilution, visual vetting by one AI analyst, a period split chosen after the detections, and no spectroscopy.
